schools.name: Classical political economy
schools.summary: Explained growth, value and distribution through labour, capital, land and competition, generally favouring freer trade over mercantilist restriction.

schools.name: Marxian economics
schools.summary: Reworked classical value theory into a critique of capitalism, focusing on class, exploitation, accumulation and recurring crises.

schools.name: Neoclassical (marginalist) economics
schools.summary: Analyses choices at the margin, with prices set by demand and supply; built the partial-equilibrium tools still used in introductory courses.

schools.name: Welfare economics
schools.summary: Asks how to judge whether one economic outcome is better than another, from social cost and externalities to social choice and capabilities.

schools.name: Keynesian and post-Keynesian economics
schools.summary: Treats aggregate demand as a driver of output and employment, so economies can settle below full employment without policy action.

schools.name: Austrian school
schools.summary: Stresses dispersed knowledge, entrepreneurship and market processes over time; sceptical of central planning and discretionary macroeconomic management.

schools.name: Monetarism and the Chicago school
schools.summary: Emphasised money supply, expectations and rules over discretion, and generally favoured markets over government intervention.

schools.name: Institutional economics and political economy
schools.summary: Explains economic outcomes through rules, property rights, norms and political power, including institutions that communities design for themselves.

schools.name: Information economics
schools.summary: Studies how asymmetric and imperfect information changes market outcomes, producing adverse selection, moral hazard, signalling and rationing.

schools.name: Experimental development economics
schools.summary: Uses randomised controlled trials and close fieldwork to test which specific policies improve the lives of poor households.

majorWork.t: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

smith.question: What makes a nation wealthy, and why do some economies grow while others stagnate?
smith.core: Wealth lies in productive labour, not stocks of gold; specialisation and competitive exchange raise output, within a framework of law, institutions and moral norms.
chain: Limited by extent of the market
smith.chainNote: This follows the order of Smith’s own argument in Book I. Linking it to later free-trade policy is a reading of his influence, not his prediction.
smith.university: History of economic thought and growth theory: specialisation and market size reappear in formal models of increasing returns and trade.
smith.relevance: Debates on global supply chains, competition policy and collusion, and the role of trust and norms in exchange still use questions Smith raised.

majorWork.t: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation

ricardo.question: How is national income divided between landlords, capitalists and workers, and how does trade affect it?
ricardo.core: Countries gain from trade by specialising according to comparative, not absolute, advantage; rising rents on scarce land can squeeze profits and slow growth.
ricardo.chainNote: The chain traces Ricardo’s trade argument and its use in the Corn Law debate; the wine and cloth example is a simplified two-good illustration.

builtOn.why: Extended Smith’s absolute-advantage case for trade to comparative advantage.

challenged.why: Disagreed with Malthus over the Corn Laws and whether a general glut of goods was possible.

ricardo.university: International trade theory: Ricardian models with many goods, technology differences and productivity, extended later by factor-endowment and new trade models.
ricardo.india: India’s post-1991 trade reforms, including the growth of services exports such as information technology, are often discussed using comparative advantage.
ricardo.relevance: Comparative advantage underpins debates about outsourcing, import competition, reshoring and industrial policy, many of which test the limits of his assumptions.

majorWork.t: An Essay on the Principle of Population

malthus.question: Can living standards rise for long if population tends to grow faster than food supply?
malthus.core: Population tends to outrun food production, so without checks on births, gains in living standards are likely to be eroded.
malthus.chainNote: This is Malthus’s own reasoning. Later growth in farm productivity and falling birth rates are the main reasons historians treat it as conditional.

challenged.why: Argued against Ricardo that a general glut of goods, from insufficient demand, was possible.

outside.name: William Godwin
outside.why: The Essay was written partly in reply to Godwin’s optimism about the improvement of society.

malthus.university: Economic history and growth theory: the ‘Malthusian trap’ appears in unified growth models explaining the long pre-industrial stagnation of living standards.
malthus.relevance: Arguments about whether natural resources and environmental limits constrain long-run growth echo Malthus; critics stress prices, substitution and innovation.

marx.question: Where do profits come from in a capitalist economy, and why is it prone to crisis?
marx.core: Profit arises from surplus value produced by labour; competition drives accumulation and mechanisation, producing inequality, concentration and recurring crises.
marx.chainNote: This sets out Marx’s argument in Capital. Whether its predictions held, and how far planned economies reflected it, are separate and contested questions.

builtOn.why: Took Ricardo’s labour theory of value and class-based account of distribution as his starting point.
Read Smith closely and reworked the classical labour theory of value.

challenged.why: Argued classical economists treated capitalism’s categories as natural rather than historically specific.

outside.name: G. W. F. Hegel
outside.why: Adapted Hegel’s dialectical method into a materialist account of history.

marx.university: Political economy and history of thought: formal debates on the transformation problem, the labour share and theories of crisis and accumulation.
marx.relevance: Debates about automation and jobs, the falling labour share and concentrated market power echo questions Marx raised, though rarely his policy conclusions.

marshall.question: How do demand and supply together determine price and quantity in a single market?
marshall.core: Price is set by demand and supply acting together, like scissor blades; marginal tools such as elasticity and consumer surplus analyse each market separately.
chain: Time periods: short and long run
marshall.chainNote: The chain shows how Marshall assembled the toolkit students use; holding other markets constant is a simplifying choice, not a description of reality.

builtOn.why: Treated his work as continuous with classical economics, joining cost of production to marginal utility.

marshall.university: Microeconomics: partial equilibrium is set against general equilibrium, and consumer surplus is derived from utility and demand functions.
marshall.relevance: Supply and demand diagrams, elasticity and surplus remain everyday tools for regulators and tax analysts; external economies help explain industrial clusters.

pigou.question: When do private decisions fail to maximise social welfare, and how could government correct them?
pigou.core: Where private and social costs or benefits diverge, markets misallocate resources; a tax or subsidy equal to the gap can improve welfare.
pigou.chainNote: The last step is later policy uptake of Pigou’s idea, shaped by many others, rather than something Pigou designed.

builtOn.why: Built welfare economics on Marshall’s consumer surplus and his idea of external effects.

outside.name: Ronald Coase
outside.why: Coase’s 1960 paper criticised the Pigouvian tax approach, stressing bargaining and transaction costs.

pigou.university: Public economics: optimal corrective taxation, comparison with tradable permits, and the Coase theorem on bargaining and property rights.
pigou.relevance: Carbon pricing, congestion charges and taxes on demerit goods apply Pigou’s reasoning; debate centres on information, feasibility and distributional effects.

majorWork.t: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money

keynes.question: Why can an economy remain stuck with mass unemployment, and what can policy do about it?
keynes.core: Output and employment depend on aggregate demand; when spending falls, an economy can settle below full employment, creating a case for policy intervention.
keynes.chainNote: The Depression framed Keynes’s argument; the final step is how governments later used it, which went beyond and sometimes differed from his own proposals.

builtOn.why: Trained in Marshall’s Cambridge economics, whose methods he used before breaking with it on aggregate demand.
Saw Malthus’s concern with general gluts as a forerunner of effective demand.

challenged.why: Cast Pigou’s theory of unemployment as the classical view the General Theory set out to replace.

outside.name: Richard Kahn
outside.why: Used Kahn’s 1931 employment multiplier in developing the General Theory.

keynes.university: Macroeconomics: IS–LM and New Keynesian models formalise demand, sticky prices and expectations; debates focus on fiscal multipliers.
keynes.india: Keynes’s first book, Indian Currency and Finance (1913), analysed India’s monetary system; he had earlier worked at the India Office in London.
keynes.relevance: Debates about stimulus, austerity, fiscal multipliers and public debt after 2008 and during COVID-19 draw directly on Keynesian reasoning.

robinson.question: How do prices, output and wages behave when firms can set prices rather than take them?
robinson.core: Most markets lie between perfect competition and monopoly; firms with market power restrict output, and employers with monopsony power can pay below marginal revenue product.
robinson.chainNote: The early steps are her 1933 book; the last summarises her later post-Keynesian work, which developed over several decades.

builtOn.why: Rebuilt Marshall’s theory of the firm for markets with price-setting firms.
Part of the Cambridge group that helped develop and extend Keynes’s theory.

outside.name: Paul Samuelson
outside.why: Opposed Samuelson and other MIT economists in the Cambridge capital controversy.

robinson.university: Industrial organisation and labour economics: formal models of oligopoly, price discrimination and monopsony wage-setting.
robinson.relevance: Debates on large digital platforms, supermarkets’ power over suppliers and minimum wages in monopsonistic labour markets use concepts she named.

majorWork.t: The Use of Knowledge in Society

hayek.question: How can an economy use knowledge that is dispersed among millions of people and held by no single mind?
hayek.core: Prices transmit dispersed, local knowledge that no planner could gather, allowing coordination without central direction; this underpins his critique of planning.
hayek.chainNote: The chain is Hayek’s own argument; critics accept the knowledge problem but question how far it rules out regulation or public provision.

builtOn.why: Developed Smith’s idea of an unplanned market order into an argument about knowledge and prices.

challenged.why: Debated Keynes in the 1930s over the causes of slumps and the role of policy.
His knowledge argument became a central objection to economies planned in Marx’s name.

outside.name: Ludwig von Mises
outside.why: Developed Mises’s critique of economic calculation under socialism.

hayek.university: Comparative economic systems and mechanism design: the socialist calculation debate and formal models of information in prices.
hayek.relevance: Relevant to debates on whether data and algorithms could support central coordination, to price-based policy design, and to credit-fuelled asset booms.

majorWork.t: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960 (with Anna Schwartz)

friedman.question: How much do changes in the money supply explain inflation and the depth of recessions?
friedman.core: Sustained inflation is mainly a monetary phenomenon; discretionary demand management is unreliable, and no lasting trade-off exists between inflation and unemployment.
friedman.chainNote: These are the main steps in Friedman’s case; the reading of the Depression is his and Schwartz’s, and remains debated alongside other explanations.

challenged.why: His monetarism was the leading challenge to postwar Keynesian demand management.

friedman.university: Monetary economics: expectations-augmented Phillips curve, the natural rate hypothesis and the rules-versus-discretion debate in central banking.
friedman.relevance: Central banks now target inflation rather than money growth, but his stress on expectations shapes their communication; 2008 responses drew on his reading of the Depression.

sen.question: What should development mean, and why do famines occur even when food is available?
sen.core: Development is the expansion of people’s real freedoms and capabilities, not income alone; famines reflect collapsing entitlements as much as falling food supply.
sen.chainNote: The steps follow Sen’s work from the 1980s to 1999; the HDI is a simplified measure inspired by his approach, not a full statement of it.

builtOn.why: Draws on Smith’s moral philosophy and his account of what people need to live without shame.

challenged.why: His entitlement analysis challenged explanations of famine based only on food supply.

outside.name: Kenneth Arrow
outside.why: Extended Arrow’s social choice theory, which Sen developed in his early work.

outside.name: Mahbub ul Haq
outside.why: The capability approach informed the Human Development Index that Haq led at the UNDP.

sen.university: Development and welfare economics: capability theory, social choice, multidimensional poverty indices and entitlement-based analysis of food crises.
sen.india: Poverty and Famines analyses the 1943 Bengal famine; his work shapes debates on Indian hunger, education, health and the HDI.
sen.relevance: Informs multidimensional poverty measures, debates about the limits of GDP per capita, and responses to hunger during food price shocks.

majorWork.t: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action

ostrom.question: Can communities manage shared resources sustainably without either state control or privatisation?
ostrom.core: Users of common pool resources can sustain them through self-designed rules, monitoring and sanctions when certain institutional conditions, her design principles, are met.
ostrom.chainNote: The chain follows her empirical programme; her design principles describe conditions associated with success, not a formula that suits every resource.

outside.name: Garrett Hardin
outside.why: Her evidence challenged Hardin’s view that commons lead to ruin without state control or privatisation.

ostrom.university: Institutional and environmental economics: game theory of collective action, repeated interaction and laboratory and field experiments on cooperation.
ostrom.india: Researchers apply her design principles to Indian groundwater, village irrigation and community forest management.
ostrom.relevance: Debates on overfishing, groundwater depletion, community forestry and climate cooperation draw on her findings about self-governance.

stiglitz.question: What happens to market outcomes when buyers, sellers, lenders and borrowers hold different information?
stiglitz.core: With imperfect and asymmetric information, markets can be inefficient, for example through credit rationing, so well-designed government action may improve outcomes.
stiglitz.chainNote: The early steps are his academic work; the last is his later application of it, set out in Globalization and Its Discontents.

challenged.why: Questioned formal invisible-hand results that rely on perfect information, rather than Smith’s own broader argument.
Challenged the view, associated with Chicago economics, that competitive markets are generally efficient.

stiglitz.university: Information economics: screening and signalling models, the Stiglitz–Weiss credit rationing model and efficiency-wage theory.
stiglitz.relevance: Insurance, credit scoring, online reviews and data privacy all raise information problems; disclosure, licensing and standards respond to them.

banerjee.question: Which specific policies actually improve the lives of poor households, and how can we know?
banerjee.core: Development questions can be broken into specific, testable problems; randomised trials and fieldwork reveal how poor households decide and which programmes work.
banerjee.chainNote: The chain describes the method he and Duflo promoted; critics question how far results from one setting transfer to others.
banerjee.university: Development economics and econometrics: causal inference, randomised evaluation, external validity and behavioural models of poor households.
banerjee.india: Born in Mumbai and raised in Kolkata, Banerjee has run many field studies in India, including education programmes with the NGO Pratham.
banerjee.relevance: Shapes how governments, charities and aid agencies design and evaluate cash transfers, school programmes, health campaigns and microfinance.

duflo.question: How can rigorous evidence identify development policies that help poor households?
duflo.core: Randomised evaluations can isolate the effects of specific policies; small design details often decide whether education, health or credit programmes succeed.
duflo.chainNote: This sets out the experimental method she helped spread; how far trial results generalise across contexts remains debated.
duflo.university: Development economics and econometrics: randomised evaluation design, causal inference and external validity of field experiments.
duflo.india: Much of her research uses trials in India, including teacher attendance monitoring with the NGO Seva Mandir in Rajasthan.
duflo.relevance: Cash transfers, women’s empowerment, education and health policy debates regularly cite experimental findings her work helped produce.

acemoglu.question: Why are some countries rich and others poor, and why do differences persist?
acemoglu.core: Inclusive economic and political institutions encourage investment and innovation; extractive institutions concentrate power and income, limiting long-run growth.
acemoglu.chainNote: The chain summarises the book’s argument; critics debate how institutions are measured and how far geography, culture or policy also matter.

outside.name: Douglass North
outside.why: Built on North’s account of institutions as the rules shaping economic incentives.

acemoglu.university: Political economy and growth: formal models of institutional change and historical natural experiments used to estimate institutional effects.
acemoglu.relevance: Shapes debates on weak institutions, corruption and the state in development; his recent work addresses technology, inequality and the labour share.

compare.title: Keynes and Hayek
compare.frame: A 1930s exchange over why slumps happen and whether governments should respond by managing demand or allow markets to adjust.

question: Why can an economy stay at high unemployment, and how can policy restore employment?
Why do booms and busts occur, and what are the limits of policy in steering a complex economy?
assumptions: Prices and wages adjust slowly; expectations and uncertainty can keep spending low for long periods.
Knowledge is dispersed; market prices coordinate plans, and credit expansion can distort the structure of production.
mechanism: Falling aggregate demand reduces output and employment, and the multiplier amplifies the fall.
Credit-driven booms misdirect investment; the bust is the economy correcting earlier distortions.
policy: Government spending and lower interest rates to support demand during a slump.
Caution about stimulus; emphasis on stable money, rules and market adjustment.
criticisms: Critics question the size of fiscal multipliers, the effect on public debt and how well governments time intervention.
Critics argue that allowing a slump to run its course imposes heavy and avoidable costs in unemployment.
context: Written during the Great Depression and published in 1936, amid mass unemployment in Britain and elsewhere.
Shaped by Austrian monetary theory; Hayek was at the London School of Economics during the 1930s debate.
relevance: Frames debates on stimulus and austerity after 2008 and during the COVID-19 response.
Cited in discussions of asset bubbles and misallocated investment after long periods of low interest rates.

compare.title: Friedman and Keynes
compare.frame: A postwar debate over what drives inflation and recessions, and whether discretionary demand management stabilises or destabilises the economy.

question: How far do changes in the money supply explain inflation and the depth of recessions?
Why can an economy remain stuck with high unemployment, and what can policy do?
assumptions: Markets tend towards a natural rate of unemployment; people adjust their inflation expectations to experience.
Uncertainty and slow-adjusting wages and prices can leave demand too low for full employment.
mechanism: Excess money growth raises inflation; attempts to hold unemployment below its natural rate only raise inflation over time.
Changes in spending alter output and employment through the multiplier, with limited automatic correction.
policy: Stable, rule-based monetary growth; scepticism about fine-tuning the economy with fiscal policy.
Active fiscal policy and low interest rates to support demand in a slump.
criticisms: Critics note that money supply targets were hard to use in practice as money demand became unstable.
Critics point to inflation in the 1970s and doubts about how accurately governments can time intervention.
context: Developed in the 1950s and 1960s and influential after stagflation in the 1970s.
Developed in response to the Great Depression and mass unemployment of the 1930s.
relevance: Central banks’ attention to inflation expectations and credibility reflects his influence.
Fiscal stimulus debates after 2008 and during COVID-19 draw on his reasoning.

compare.title: Smith and Marx
compare.frame: Two readings of a market economy: one stressing specialisation and growth through exchange, the other stressing class relations, exploitation and crisis.

question: What makes a nation wealthy, and how do markets coordinate production without central direction?
Where do profits come from under capitalism, and why is it prone to inequality and crisis?
assumptions: Self-interest operates within law, competition and moral norms; productive labour is the source of wealth.
Labour creates value; the relationship between owners of capital and wage workers shapes distribution.
mechanism: Division of labour raises productivity, and competition guides resources through prices towards what people want.
Capitalists gain surplus value from labour; competition drives accumulation, mechanisation and concentration.
policy: Removing monopoly privileges and trade restrictions, with the state providing defence, justice and public works.
Replacing capitalist ownership of the means of production, an argument made more in his political writing.
criticisms: Critics argue he underrated market power, inequality and instability, though he warned about collusion himself.
Critics reject the labour theory of value and point to the economic record of centrally planned states.
context: Enlightenment Scotland in the 1770s, writing against mercantilist trade policy and chartered monopolies.
Industrialising Britain and Europe in the mid-nineteenth century, amid harsh factory conditions.
relevance: Supply chains, competition policy and the role of trust in exchange still draw on his questions.
Debates on automation, the labour share and concentrated market power echo themes he raised.

compare.title: Pigou and Coase
compare.frame: Two approaches to externalities: correcting them with taxes and subsidies, or allowing affected parties to bargain once property rights are clear.

question: When private and social costs diverge, how can government move output to the socially optimal level?
When one party’s activity harms another, can the parties reach an efficient outcome through bargaining?
assumptions: Government can measure the external cost well enough to set a corrective tax or subsidy.
Property rights are clearly defined, and the costs of negotiating and enforcing agreements are low.
mechanism: A tax equal to the marginal external cost raises the private cost to the social cost.
Affected parties trade rights; with low transaction costs, the efficient outcome can follow whoever holds the rights.
policy: Taxes on activities with negative externalities and subsidies for those with positive externalities.
Clear property rights and attention to transaction costs; government action compared case by case.
criticisms: Critics stress the information needed to set the right tax and the political pressures on tax setting.
Critics note that many externalities involve many parties, making bargaining costly or impractical.
context: Developed at Cambridge in the early twentieth century, building on Marshall’s welfare analysis.
Set out in The Problem of Social Cost (1960), partly as a critique of the Pigouvian approach.
relevance: Underlies carbon taxes, congestion charges and taxes on demerit goods.
Informs tradable permit schemes and legal approaches to nuisance, pollution and property rights.

compare.title: Capabilities and income measures
compare.frame: Whether development is best measured by income or GDP per capita, or by what people are actually able to do and be.

question: What real freedoms and opportunities do people have to live lives they value?
How much output and income does an economy produce per person, and how fast is it growing?
assumptions: People convert income into well-being at different rates, depending on health, gender, disability and environment.
Income is a useful general measure of command over goods and services, and of the means to well-being.
mechanism: Development expands capabilities such as health, education and political freedom, which are valued in themselves.
Rising income per head allows higher consumption and funds health, education and public services.
policy: Investment in health, education, social protection and democratic participation alongside growth.
Policies that raise productivity, investment and output, with income growth as the main target.
criticisms: Critics argue capabilities are hard to select, weight and measure, and that composite indices simplify the approach.
Critics argue averages hide inequality and omit non-market activity, health, freedom and environmental damage.
context: Developed from the late 1970s onwards, informed by Sen’s study of famines and welfare economics.
National income accounting developed in the 1930s and 1940s and became the standard development benchmark.
relevance: Underlies the Human Development Index and multidimensional poverty measures.
GDP per capita remains the most widely used single indicator for comparing living standards across countries.
